title: ADHD vs anxiety: how to tell the difference
summary: ADHD and anxiety share symptoms but have different drivers. Learn what separates them, why they get confused, and how providers tell them apart.
body_markdown:
ADHD and anxiety can look identical from the outside, but they’re driven by different things. ADHD is a persistent difficulty in regulating your attention, and it begins in childhood. Anxiety is excessive worry about a perceived threat, and that can start at any age.


[About 6.0% of U.S. adults had a current ADHD diagnosis in 2023](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/wr/mm7340a1.htm) . More than half of them were diagnosed after turning 18. If you’re searching “ADHD vs anxiety,” you’ve probably read a list of the symptoms present in both conditions and wondered about what you’re experiencing.


We treat both conditions at Circle Medical. You can talk through[an online ADHD treatment from board-certified providers](https://www.circlemedical.com/what-we-treat/adhd) or online anxiety treatment.


## ADHD vs anxiety: the short answer


The core difference between ADHD and Anxiety is what pulls your attention off a task.


In ADHD, your attention follows your interest and level of stimulation, so you might procrastinate when faced with a boring task stalls while staying engaged for hours on a task that interests you.


In anxiety, your attention follows a sense of threat, so your concentration drops while part of your mind rehearses what might go wrong.


## ADHD vs anxiety at a glance


-


**Core difference:** ADHD is an ongoing difficulty regulating attention. Anxiety is excessive worry about a perceived threat.


-


**Onset:** ADHD symptoms appear before age 12. Anxiety can begin at any age, including adulthood.


-


**Shared symptoms:** Six symptoms overlap, including restlessness, trouble concentrating, and irritability.


-


**Prevalence:**[19.1% of U.S. adults had an anxiety disorder in the past year, compared with 4.4% current adult ADHD prevalence.](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/statistics/any-anxiety-disorder)


-


**Overlap:**[Anxiety rates in adults with ADHD run 4.3% to 47.1%, versus 0.5% to 9.5% in adults without ADHD .](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9635752/)


Dimension ADHD Anxiety


**What it is** A neurodevelopmental condition affecting attention, impulse control, and activity level A group of conditions involving excessive worry, fear, or dread


**What pulls attention away** Interest, novelty, and urgency A perceived threat, current or anticipated


**When symptoms start** Several symptoms present before age 12 Any age, including adulthood


**Where it shows up** Two or more settings, such as work and home Often tied to specific triggers, though generalized anxiety spreads wider


**What the mind is doing** Attention moves between unrelated topics Worry circles back to the same feared outcome


**Common physical signs** Restlessness, fidgeting, fast speech Muscle tension, racing heart, stomach upset, fatigue


**On a task you find interesting** Focus can become intense and sustained Worry often continues regardless of the task


**Duration used in diagnosis** Symptoms persist at least 6 months and impair functioning Generalized anxiety is defined by excessive worry occurring most days through at least a period of 6 months.


## Symptoms that look the same


Six symptoms turn up in both conditions. These include trouble concentrating, restlessness, irritability, sleep problems, procrastination, and forgetfulness.


Four of those six appear in the DSM-5 criteria for generalized anxiety disorder, and restlessness and inattention sit at the center of ADHD.


The CDC notes that there is[“no single test to diagnose ADHD,” and other conditions “can also have symptoms similar to ADHD,”](https://www.cdc.gov/adhd/diagnosis/index.html) including sleep disorders and anxiety.


Shared symptom How it often looks in ADHD How it often looks in anxiety


Trouble concentrating Attention drifts toward whatever is more stimulating, even on a calm day Concentration drops because worry is using the available bandwidth


Restlessness A physical need to move, fidget, or stand up An internal sense of being keyed up or on edge


Irritability Often follows frustration, interruption, or overstimulation Often follows sustained tension and poor sleep


Sleep problems Difficulty winding down and going to bed on time Difficulty falling asleep because the worry keeps running


Procrastination Starting is hard because the task offers no urgency or interest, sometimes called[ADHD paralysis](https://add.org/adhd-paralysis/) Starting is hard because of excessive worry that the task might go badly


Forgetfulness Information doesn’t stay in working memory long enough to be used Attention was on the worry, so the information never registered


### ADHD symptoms start before age 12, while anxiety can start at any age


The onset of your symptoms is what your medical provider will lean on the hardest. Diagnostic criteria require several ADHD symptoms before age 12.


Anxiety carries no equivalent childhood requirement. If your concentration was fine through your twenties and fell apart at 34, ADHD becomes less likely. If your third-grade report cards mention daydreaming, that’s behavioral history that counts.


### ADHD spreads across settings, and anxiety often clusters around triggers


ADHD symptoms typically appear in two or more settings, like work, home, and friendships. Anxiety can be just as pervasive, but it often clusters around identifiable triggers like performance, health, or social situations.


Generalized anxiety disorder is the exception, since the worry spreads across many areas at once. Where your symptoms don’t appear can be as telling as where they do.


### Physical symptoms between ADHD and anxiety differ


ADHD restlessness is usually visible. You might fidget, tap, or pace. Anxiety restlessness is more internal, like a feeling of being wound up.


Anxiety also brings muscle tension, a racing heart, and stomach upset more consistently than ADHD does. Fatigue is common in anxiety because the body stays on alert. ADHD fatigue tends to come from mental overstimulation rather than physical tension.


If these differences point toward one condition more than the other, a primary care provider can help you sort through the details. ## ADHD vs generalized anxiety disorder


Generalized anxiety disorder is the condition most often confused with ADHD. Three symptoms of GAD can overlap with ADHD: restlessness, difficulty concentrating, and irritability.


A diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive worry “occurring more days than not for at least 6 months” and difficulty controlling that worry. It also requires three or more of six symptoms: restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance.


The difference comes down to worry: GAD requires persistent worry, while ADHD does not. ADHD can leave you buried under a backlog with no accompanying dread about the future.


Feature ADHD Generalized anxiety disorder


**Required core feature** Persistent inattention, hyperactivity, or impulsivity Excessive worry that’s difficult to control


**Restlessness** A core hyperactivity symptom One of six supporting symptoms


**Difficulty concentrating** A core inattention symptom One of six supporting symptoms


**Irritability** Commonly reported, not a listed criterion One of six supporting symptoms


**Time requirement** At least 6 months, with several symptoms before age 12 Worry more days than not for at least 6 months


## Why getting the distinction right changes treatment


ADHD care and anxiety care aim at different targets.


ADHD care typically works on the executive function side: structure, routines, and support for planning, task initiation, and follow-through, with medication when clinically appropriate. The goal is to make daily systems hold up rather than to reduce worry.


Anxiety care typically works on the worry itself, through therapy approaches, sleep and lifestyle changes, and medication when clinically appropriate. The goal is to bring the threat response down so you can go back to concentrating on your tasks.


An expensive mistake many adults make is treating the more visible condition for years while the less obvious one goes unaddressed. Anxiety is easier to name, so it often gets treated first. Attention problems that persist afterward are useful information instead of a sign that the treatment failed.

## ADHD vs anxiety FAQs


### Is it ADHD or anxiety?


A comprehensive evaluation can answer that. A provider looks at when your symptoms started, where they appear, and what your attention does when you’re engaged versus worried.


Symptoms present before age 12 point toward ADHD. Worry that’s hard to control for six months or more points toward an anxiety disorder.


### Can anxiety mimic ADHD symptoms?


Yes, and often. Anxiety can produce difficulty concentrating, restlessness, irritability, and sleep problems, all of which are associated with ADHD too.


Difficulty concentrating appears in the DSM-5 criteria for generalized anxiety disorder directly. Onset is the usual separator, since anxiety-driven concentration problems tend to begin alongside a stressful period.


### Is anxiety a symptom of ADHD?


Anxiety is a separate condition rather than an ADHD symptom, and the two co-occur often. Anxiety can also develop as a consequence of living with unmanaged ADHD, since repeated missed deadlines create real worry about your own reliability.


A provider can help sort out which came first, which usually takes a timeline.


### Can you be diagnosed with both ADHD and anxiety?


Yes, and it’s common. A 2022 systematic review in PLOS ONE found anxiety disorder rates in adults with ADHD ranging from 4.3% to 47.1% in general-population studies.


Diagnosing one condition doesn’t rule out the other, and a comprehensive evaluation assesses both. If you meet criteria for both, your care plan can address both.


### Can ADHD make anxiety worse?


Living with untreated ADHD can create anxiety about performance, deadlines, and reliability. The stress of managing symptoms without support often builds over time.


Treating the ADHD may ease that downstream anxiety, though some people have a separate anxiety disorder that needs its own care. A provider can tell the difference.


### Do free online ADHD vs anxiety tests work?


Free tests can help you organize what you’re experiencing, and they can’t distinguish the two conditions. Most quizzes borrow items from screeners like the ASRS or GAD-7 without the clinical interpretation those instruments need.


They also can’t verify childhood onset or rule out thyroid problems, sleep disorders, and other causes of similar symptoms.


### Does treating one improve the other?


Sometimes, depending on which condition is driving your symptoms. When anxiety is primary, treating it may resolve the concentration problems that looked like ADHD.


When ADHD is primary and anxiety developed downstream, treating the ADHD may ease the anxiety over time. Your provider can track how your symptoms respond.


### Which is more common in adults?


Anxiety is more common. NIMH reports that 19.1% of U.S. adults had any anxiety disorder in the past year, against a current adult ADHD prevalence of 4.4% in the same survey program.


The CDC’s 2023 survey estimated 6.0% of U.S. adults had a current ADHD diagnosis. Both are frequently undiagnosed in adults.


## Book an ADHD or anxiety consultation today


You can’t settle this question alone because you need a thorough evaluation of your history, not just your current symptoms. You can personally observe your onset of symptoms, how it spreads across different settings, and what your attention does depending on your interests versus the feeling of threat.


But turning those observations into a diagnosis takes a provider who can weigh them against your medical history.


So bring those observations to a medical provider. If the past few months have been the worst of your experiences, start there. If you’ve felt this way since school, say so out loud at your appointment, because it changes the conversation immediately.


Seek care sooner if your symptoms are interfering with work, school, or relationships. The same applies if you’re experiencing panic attacks, thoughts of self-harm, or symptoms that are worsening quickly.
